extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of humor theory, literary critics, and philosophers of art
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying Henri Bergson's conceptual criteria for what makes something comic — the kinds of absurdity, mental mechanisms, social functions, and dramatic techniques that produce laughter. Useful for analysing comic scenes, characters, or building comic effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrast between particular (professional) logic and universal logic
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain ways of reasoning are customary and valid within particular circles (a 'professional logic') but untrue or absurd to the general public; the contrast between these two kinds of logic produces comic effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Moliere's Femmes savantes (scientific ideas translated into 'feminine sensibility')—the humour arises when specialised reasoning is transposed into ordinary social interaction. Use scenes where a specialized mode of thought is applied outside its proper context to create comic friction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic involves a particular kind of absurdity, not absurdity in general
rubrics_metrics.description: Absurdity, when present in the comic, is not 'absurdity in general' but an absurdity of a definite, characteristic kind infused by the comic itself; it is an effect that reflects the special nature of its cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid treating any random irrationality as comic; the laughable requires a specific relation to common sense and social norms (see inversion of common sense, automatism). Construct jokes so the absurdity stems from a definable departure from expected reasoning or behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inversion of common sense (moulding things to ideas)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic arises when a person seeks to mould things to an idea in their head rather than adapting their ideas to actual things — e.g., Don Quixote seeing giants where others see windmills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dramatise characters whose privileged recollection/idea dominates perception, producing misinterpretation of ordinary objects/events. The comedy comes from the logical follow-through of that misperception (the character acts with somnambulistic certainty).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigidity/automatism/obstinacy of mind (the single-minded character)
rubrics_metrics.description: At the root of the comic is a kind of rigidity that compels victims to keep strictly to one path: A CHARACTER FOLLOWING UP HIS ONE IDEA and continually recurring to it in spite of interruptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create characters who persistently repeat or pursue one idea despite context changes; comedic scenes often reduce to this single dynamic. The humour increases as the character progressively shuts out contrary evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dream-logic similarity (relaxation of rules of reasoning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic illusion is similar to dream illusion; reasonings we laugh at are those we know to be false but might accept in a dream. Dream-logic features relaxed reasoning, surface logical links, and toleration of contradictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use images, sequences, or dialogues that follow a dream-like associative logic (abridged reasonings, surface connections). The result should counterfeit reasoning enough to be recognisable yet lax enough to grant relief from intellectual tension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abridged or superficial reasoning leading toward word-play
rubrics_metrics.description: Many 'witticisms' are considerably abridged reasonings given only as beginning and end; as the relations between ideas become more superficial, play upon ideas evolves into play upon words (sound over meaning).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design punchlines that depend on compressed logical leaps or punning where the audience mentally supplies omitted steps. Beware: if the leap is too large or not recognisable as an abridgement, it will fail to be funny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic obsessions and repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: Repetition of the same image or phrase across contexts (comic obsessions) resembles dream repetition; a burden of a song or a recurring image can persist, each time taking on a different (comical) meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ repeated motifs or refrains that recur with shifting interpretations. The humour often depends on the audience recognising the recurrence and the incongruity of meanings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crescendo toward absurdity (progressive escalation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A sequence in which one concession to absurdity introduces another, each more serious, until crowning absurdity is reached — producing a growing sensation similar to a dream's escalation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure scenes to escalate: small illogicalities accumulate logically (in the character's mind) into increasingly extravagant situations. Examples: Moliere's Monsieur de Pourceaugnac and Bourgeois gentilhomme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confusion/fusion of identities (self and other blending)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dream-like fusions where a person is both himself and someone else, or where the speaker shifts perspective (e.g., Mark Twain's dialogue where the narrator treats himself as a third person) — this confusion produces a distinctive comic absurdity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use narrative or dialogue devices that blur subjectivity (first/third person confusion, mistaken identity, doubling) to produce a specific, dream-like absurdity. Ensure the listener can detect that the absurdity arises from identity confusion rather than mere nonsense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial sympathy/relaxation followed by corrective humiliation
rubrics_metrics.description: The laugher initially sympathises — briefly adopting the comic character's gestures or play — which relaxes intellectual tension; but laughter's social function is corrective and humiliating, aiming to punish impertinences toward society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design comic moments to invite a short-lived identification (letting the audience 'join in the game') and then withdraw to reveal the corrective sting. Balance warmth/identification with the eventual distancing needed for the social corrective to function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughter as spontaneous, often unjust social corrective
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter is largely spontaneous, a mechanism set up by nature or social habit; it punishes by humiliating and cannot be absolutely just because it is not the product of reflection — it strikes for a general result while missing individual nuance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analysing comedy, consider its social corrective intent and its lack of deliberation: laughter may target innocents and miss true culpability. For creators, be aware that spontaneous laughter can wound; for critics, account for the social dynamics that produce laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic effect as relief from intellectual tension (playfulness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Deep-rooted in the comic is a tendency to take the line of least resistance; comic absurdity invites us to 'take it easy' and join in play, thereby providing relief from the strain of thinking and living.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use comic devices that lower cognitive effort (rhythm, repeated patterns, familiar schemas subverted) to induce pleasurable relaxation. The audience's temporary suspension of rigorous attention is part of the effect; maintain a balance so the relief doesn't turn into mere confusion.
